title: Patient characteristics to guide personalized treatment decisions and prognostication in hepatocellular carcinoma

paragraphs.en: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for approximately 90% of primary liver cancer cases and is the fourth leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with over a million annual deaths predicted by 2030 [1]. The global burden of hepatocellular carcinoma continues to rise, with marked geographic variability reflecting differences in underlying etiologies and screening practices [2]. About 90% of HCC cases are seen in cirrhotic livers, which are typically associated with obesity, alcoholism and chronic hepatitis infections [3]. As the etiologic landscape changes due to public health initiatives like HBV vaccination and HCV antiviral therapy, an epidemiological shift toward non-viral causes is beginning to emerge [4,5]. Moreover, the global rise in obesity as a pandemic disease due to sedentary lifestyle and changing dietary habits has resulted in an increasing prevalence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and its progression to cirrhosis [4,5]. Despite advances in surveillance strategies, a substantial proportion of patients continue to present with advanced-stage disease, limiting the applicability of curative therapies such as resection, transplantation, or ablation. Consequently, HCC remains a major contributor to global cancer-related mortality, with disproportionately poor outcomes in resource-limited settings.

HCC is unique among solid malignancies because treatment decisions must account for both tumor burden and underlying liver function. Tumor burden should be characterized using reproducible imaging metrics. RECIST 1.1, which is commonly used in prospective systemic therapy trials, evaluates changes in the size of selected target lesions, whereas modified RECIST (mRECIST) evaluates viable HCC by measuring the arterial-phase enhancing component of the tumor [6,7]. Volumetric tumor measurements may provide additional information but remain less standardized for routine systemic treatment decisions

Most patients develop HCC in the setting of chronic liver disease or cirrhosis. Additionally, the liver represents an immunologically distinct organ characterized by a tolerogenic microenvironment, which facilitates immune evasion and tumor progression. This dual dependence on tumor biology and host liver function distinguishes HCC from most other malignancies and underpins the need for personalized therapeutic strategies. The immune microenvironment of HCC may also vary by underlying etiology. MASLD/MASH associated HCC has been associated with dysfunctional or exhausted CD8-positive T-cell populations and impaired antitumor immune surveillance, whereas viral associated HCC may exhibit a more antigen driven inflammatory milieu [8,9]. However, substantial biological heterogeneity exists within each etiologic group, and contemporary randomized trial subgroup analyses have not established viral or non-viral etiology as a validated biomarker for selecting ICI therapy.

The evolution of frontline systemic therapy for HCC has been driven by a series of landmark clinical trials that have progressively reshaped the treatment landscape [10–16]. As a result, the current frontline setting has become increasingly complex and enriched with multiple therapeutic options. While several recent reviews have summarized the efficacy and safety of individual systemic therapies, there remains a lack of comprehensive, clinically oriented framework that integrate tumor characteristics, liver function, patient comorbidities, and evolving therapeutic evidence into a unified decision-making approach. In particular, the practical application of trial data to heterogeneous real-world patient populations is insufficiently addressed in the existing literature. In this manuscript, we provide a discussion of these key clinical and prognostic considerations that should be assessed when selecting optimal management strategies.

This narrative review was based on a targeted literature search conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE and major hepatology and oncology conference proceedings, including the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL), and the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD). The search covered publications from January 2008 through March 2025.

Search terms included combinations of “hepatocellular carcinoma,” “advanced HCC,” “immune checkpoint inhibitors,” “atezolizumab,” “bevacizumab,” “durvalumab,” “tremelimumab,” “nivolumab,” “ipilimumab,” “sorafenib,” “lenvatinib,” “Child-Pugh,” “ALBI,” “portal hypertension,” “varices,” “portal vein tumor thrombosis,” “cardiovascular disease,” “autoimmune disease,” “liver transplantation,” “prognostic factors,” and “treatment selection.”

As this manuscript was designed as a narrative review rather than a systematic review, formal inclusion and exclusion criteria were not prespecified. Priority was given to phase II and III clinical trials, guideline recommendations, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and high-quality real-world studies evaluating patient-specific prognostic factors and treatment outcomes.

The real-world evidence included in this review was heterogeneous in design and methodological quality, ranging from prospective multicenter registries to retrospective single-center cohorts. Interpretation considered sample size, patient selection, geographic setting, treatment era, completeness of follow-up, consistency of outcome definitions, and the potential for confounding by indication, immortal-time bias, and missing data. Because a formal risk-of-bias tool was not applied, real-world estimates were considered complementary and hypothesis-generating and were not assigned the same evidentiary weight as randomized clinical-trial results. Reported efficacy and safety outcomes were extracted directly from original publications and interpreted within the context of individual study design and eligibility criteria.

Historically, systemic treatment options for advanced HCC were limited, and outcomes remained poor despite multiple therapeutic attempts. Traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy has demonstrated limited efficacy and is associated with a substantial toxicity burden, particularly in patients with underlying cirrhosis. These safety concerns, coupled with marginal survival benefits, have largely limited the role of conventional chemotherapy in the management of HCC.

Sorafenib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, which targets the VEGFR 1–3, PDGFR-β, and RAF-MEK-ERK signaling cascade [10,17,18]. It was approved as a systemic therapy for advanced HCC based on SHARP trial [3,10]. This trial demonstrated a median overall survival (mOS) of 10.7 months (95% CI 9.4–13.3) versus 7.9 months with placebo (95% CI 6.8–9.1; HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55–0.87) and median progression free survival (PFS) of 5.5 months (95% CI 4.1–6.9) versus 2.8 months (95% CI 2.7–3.9); HR 0.58 (95% CI 0.45–0.74) [10]. This was a significant 31% relative reduction in the hazard of death and a 2.8-month absolute improvement in median overall survival. Thus, the benefit was clinically meaningful in a setting with no effective systemic alternative, although the absolute median survival gain remained modest. For more than a decade, sorafenib was the only approved frontline systemic therapy for unresectable HCC [10,17,18].

The REFLECT trial evaluated lenvatinib, an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting VEGFR 1–3, FGFR 1–4, PDGFR-α, RET, and KIT, as a non-inferior treatment option to sorafenib, demonstrating mOS of 13.6 months (95% CI 12.1–14.9) versus 12.3 months with sorafenib (95% CI 10.4–13.9; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79–1.06), while also significantly prolonging PFS to 7.4 months (95% CI 6.9–8.8) vs 3.7 months (95% CI 3.6–4.6); HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.57–0.77) [3,12, 19–21].

Systemic therapy for advanced HCC has experienced a major shift in the last decade with the advent of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) [11–14,22,23]. This paradigm shift was largely driven by the landmark, practice changing IMbrave150 trial, which demonstrated that the combination of atezolizumab and bevacizumab significantly improved overall and progression survival outcomes compared to sorafenib [15]. Atezolizumab is a PD-L1 inhibitor that restores antitumor T-cell activity, while bevacizumab is a VEGF-A monoclonal antibody that inhibits angiogenesis and reduces VEGF-mediated immunosuppression [15]. VEGF-A blockade can transiently normalize vascular architecture and perfusion, increase immune-cell adhesion and T-cell trafficking, and reduce VEGF-mediated immunosuppression, thereby creating a more immune-permissive environment for PD-L1 blockade [15]. It was the first combination that demonstrated a significant improvement in mOS 19.2 months [95% CI 17.0–23.7] versus 13.4 months [95% CI 11.4–16.9]; HR 0.66 [95% CI 0.52–0.85]) and mPFS 6.9 months [95% CI 5.7–8.6] versus 4.3 months [95% CI 4.0–5.6]; HR 0.65 [95% CI 0.53–0.81] compared to sorafenib [15,16]. The combination also provided better quality of life compared to sorafenib [15]. However, given the anti-angiogenic effects of bevacizumab, careful patient selection is required due to an increased risk of bleeding, particularly in those with portal hypertension and esophageal varices.

Dual immune checkpoint inhibition of programmed death-1 (PD-1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) emerged as a promising strategy in the management of HCC based on the phase III HIMALAYA trial [24]. CTLA-4 inhibition enhances T-cell priming in lymphoid tissues, while PD-1/PD-L1 blockade restores exhausted effector T cells in the tumor microenvironment leading to durable antitumor responses [24]. The STRIDE (Single Tremelimumab Regular Interval Durvalumab) regimen demonstrated superior mOS of 16.4 months (95% CI 14.2–19.6) compared to 13.8 months (95% CI 12.3–16.1) with sorafenib; HR 0.78 (96.02% CI 0.65–0.93) [25]. At 3 years, STRIDE achieved 30.7% survival vs 20.2% with sorafenib, and 5-year follow up confirmed OS of 19.6% vs 9.4% [26].

CheckMate 040 and CheckMate 9DW trials further established the efficacy of dual immune checkpoint inhibition [27,28]. In CheckMate 040, the combination of nivolumab (anti-PD-1) and ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) was evaluated across different dosing regimens in patients who were either intolerant to or had progressed on sorafenib [28]. The most effective dosing arm—nivolumab 1 mg/kg + ipilimumab 3 mg/kg every 3 weeks ×4 followed by nivolumab 240 mg every 2 weeks achieved an objective response rate (ORR) of 31% [28]. Building on these results, a randomized phase III trial (CheckMate 9DW) was designed to compare this nivolumab-ipilimumab combination against investigator’s choice of lenvatinib or sorafenib in the frontline management of advanced or metastatic HCC patients. Patients received four induction doses of ipilimumab compared to only one induction dose of tremelimumab in HIMALAYA [28]. Results demonstrated a mOS of 23.7 months (95% CI 18.8–29.4) vs 20.6 months (95% CI 17.5–22.5); HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.65–0.96) [28]. Interestingly, mPFS was nearly identical 9.1 months (95% CI 6.6–10.5) vs 9.2 months (95% CI 7.9–11.1); HR 0·87 (0·72–1·06) [28]. While 12-month OS was comparable between arms, landmark analyses showed 24-month OS 49% vs 39% and 36-month OS 38% vs 24% [28]. The similar median PFS but progressive separation of the overall-survival curves likely reflects a delayed “long-tail” immunotherapy effect rather than superior early disease control across the entire population.

Safety comparisons between dual-ICI regimens should be interpreted cautiously because trials used different definitions and follow-up periods for immune-mediated adverse events. In HIMALAYA, immune-mediated adverse events of any grade occurred in 35.8% of STRIDE-treated patients, and grade 3–4 immune-mediated events occurred in approximately 13% [29]. CheckMate 9DW did not report an identical aggregate immune-mediated event endpoint. However, grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 53% with nivolumab-ipilimumab. These indirect comparisons suggest that the four-dose ipilimumab induction regimen may carry a greater overall severe-toxicity burden, but they do not constitute a randomized comparison of the two dual-ICI regimens

Long-term toxicity remains an underexplored but clinically important issue with ICI-TKI combinations in HCC. In LEAP-002, grade 3–5 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 62.8% of patients receiving lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab, versus 58.0% with lenvatinib plus placebo [30]. Long-term follow-up did not identify new safety signals, suggesting that toxicity is substantial but largely consistent with known ICI and VEGF/TKI-related effects [31]. Importantly, immune-related adverse events are not limited to the early treatment period, ASCO notes that they may occur or recur months after discontinuation of ICIs [32]. In fact, the newer survivorship literature emphasizes that many chronic irAEs can persist well beyond treatment cessation [32]. In practice, late management requires structured long-term surveillance for endocrine, hepatic, dermatologic, and gastrointestinal toxicities.

Management of late immune-related toxicity should be organ-specific. Endocrine toxicities require continued surveillance with thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine testing, with additional evaluation of the adrenal and pituitary axes when clinically indicated. Established hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency is generally managed with long-term hormone replacement, and immunotherapy may often be resumed once the patient is clinically stable. In contrast, suspected immune-mediated hepatitis requires exclusion of tumor progression, biliary obstruction, viral hepatitis or reactivation, ischemic injury, and other hepatotoxic medications. Immunotherapy should be held and corticosteroids initiated according to severity. Mycophenolate may be considered for steroid-refractory hepatitis, and infliximab is generally avoided because of potential hepatotoxicity. Recurrent severe or grade 4 hepatitis usually warrants permanent ICI discontinuation. Because HCC-specific survivorship data for ICI-TKI combinations remain limited, many long-term management principles are still extrapolated from broader irAE guidelines and pan-tumor survivorship experience rather than dedicated HCC datasets [32].

Based on the results of landmark trials of IMBRAVE-150, HIMALAYA and CheckMate9DW, three ICI-based combinations namely, atezolizumab-bevacizumab, durvalumab-tremelimumab, and nivolumab-ipilimumab, are now frontline treatment options for patients with advanced/metastatic HCC [28,33–36] (Table 1).

Taken together, these results show two distinct patterns: atezolizumab-bevacizumab offers early and durable benefit, while dual ICI strategies such as STRIDE and ipilimumab-nivolumab demonstrated long-term survival outcomes. This divergence of early attrition versus long-term benefit, underscores a central challenge that not all patients are equally likely to reach the survival plateau. These underscore the importance of prognostication and identifying clinical and disease related factors that can help predict which patients may achieve prolonged survival [38].

Etiology-specific differences may influence treatment response in HCC and represent an important consideration in personalized therapy. Subgroup analyses from the IMbrave150 trial demonstrated improved OS and PFS across major etiologic subgroups, including HBV, HCV, and non-viral disease, supporting its broad applicability. Similarly, outcomes from the HIMALAYA trial were consistent across etiologies. However, emerging evidence from meta-analyses and retrospective studies suggests that the patients with non-viral HCC, particularly those with MASLD, may derive comparatively less benefit from ICIs than those with viral-associated HCC, potentially related to differences in the tumor immune microenvironment [8]. While these findings are not yet practice-changing, they highlight the importance of considering disease etiology in treatment selection and the need for further prospective validation.

Most pivotal trials enrolled patients with compensated cirrhosis (Child Pugh A (CPA)), favorable performance status (ECOG 0–1), no significant bleeding risk and/or prior liver transplant [10–12,14,15,22,28]. This selective eligibility means that trial results may not fully reflect the heterogeneity of real-world patients. Knowing these factors in advance is important for guiding personalized management strategies [34]. Clinical decision-making must consider the degree of hepatic failure, portal hypertension, previous variceal hemorrhage, the existence of comorbidities, and logistical limitations such as treatment accessibility. Prognostic tools such as the CP score and ALBI grade help stratify patients and predict clinical outcomes [33].

sections.title: Treatment landscape post progression on ICIs

paragraphs.en: The advent of ICI’s has shifted the treatment paradigm, leading to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) now being more commonly utilized in the second line and subsequent settings following disease progression on ICIs. After progression on an ICI, the current NCCN guidelines recommend lenvatinib, cabozantinib, regorafenib, and ramucirumab (for AFP ≥ 400 ng/mL), while sorafenib is rarely considered [36]. However, the optimal sequence after progression on ICI remains undefined.

Following progression on ICI therapy, sequencing strategies remain an area of active investigation with limited prospective data. In clinical practice, TKIs are most commonly utilized after ICI failure, however, the optimal sequence and timing remain uncertain. Lenvatinib has demonstrated reproducible efficacy in the post-ICI setting. In a multicenter Japanese cohort of 101 patients receiving lenvatinib post atezolizumab-bevacizumab, mPFS was 4.4 months and mOS 15.7 months [39]. Among CPA patients, PFS had improved to 4.7 months while OS was not reached [39]. Interestingly, outcomes were affected by hepatic reserve. Cabozantinib (a VEGFR, MET, and AXL inhibitor) demonstrated improvement in mOS (10.2 vs 8.0 months; HR 0.76) and mPFS (5.2 vs 1.9 months; HR 0.44) compared to placebo in the CELESTIAL trial (pre-ICI era) [13]. More recently, real-world post-ICI data confirms preserved activity. In a large international retrospective cohort of patients progressing on ICIs, cabozantinib achieved mOS of 14.3 months and mPFS of 4.3 months [40]. Its unique mechanism may help overcome VEGF-related resistance by targeting MET/AXL signaling [41]. Cabozantinib inhibits VEGFR2 as well as MET and AXL, pathways implicated in tumor invasion, epithelial mesenchymal transition, immune evasion, and adaptive resistance to antiangiogenic therapy. Its broader target profile therefore provides a mechanistic rationale for activity after bevacizumab or lenvatinib containing therapy. Nevertheless, current clinical data demonstrate post-ICI activity rather than proving that MET/AXL inhibition specifically reverses acquired resistance to prior VEGF blockade.

Ramucirumab (a monoclonal antibody that targets VEGFR-2) is the only biomarker selected systemic therapy in advanced HCC, indicated for patients with baseline AFP ≥ 400 ng/mL [41]. In the phase III REACH-2 trial (pre-ICI era), ramucirumab improved mOS to 8.5 vs 7.3 months post progression on sorafenib [41]. Real-world reports suggest activity post-ICI, with mOS of 7.5 months and mPFS of 3.9 months following atezolizumab-bevacizumab [42]. Regorafenib (a VEGFR, FGFR, RET, KIT, and RAF kinase inhibitor) was studied in the RESORCE trial (pre-ICI) [11]. Patients with prior sorafenib tolerance achieved mOS of 10.6 vs 7.8 months and mPFS 3.1 vs 1.5 months [11]. In the post-ICI era, the REGONEXT phase II trial, regorafenib yielded a median PFS of 3.5 months and median OS of 9.7 months in patients who progressed on atezolizumab-bevacizumab [43].

In real-world practice, treatment selection in the post-ICI setting is further complicated by progressive decline in hepatic function and performance status, which may limit eligibility for subsequent lines of therapy. Additionally, prior exposure to bevacizumab may influence the choice and efficacy of subsequent anti-angiogenic agents, although robust prospective comparative data is lacking.

These data highlight that TKIs remain the cornerstone of systemic therapy following ICI progression. Choice among agents should be guided by hepatic reserve, performance status, prior TKI tolerance, and AFP status. The lack of validated sequencing strategies underscores the need for individualized treatment approaches.

Given this heterogeneity, personalized approaches incorporating patient-specific prognostic factors have become essential for optimizing therapeutic outcomes. The goal of this review is to synthesize the current evidence on frontline systemic therapy for HCC, with an emphasis on integrating patient-specific characteristics into therapeutic decision making. We intend to provide a practical framework to guide individualized therapy selection for patients with advanced HCC (Figure 1).

As the frontline treatment landscape continues to evolve and define the standards of care, real world clinical management often involves patients that do not meet trial eligibility criteria. Treatment selection, tolerability, and outcomes are influenced by a variety of patient and disease related factors. This section highlights special scenarios where individualized prognostication guides clinical decision-making (Figure 1).

Prognostic assessment in HCC extends beyond baseline risk stratification and plays a critical role in guiding treatment eligibility, transitions between lines of therapy, and clinical trial selection. While the Child-Pugh classification remains widely used, emerging evidence supports the Albumin-Bilirubin (ALBI) grade as a more objective tool for assessing hepatic reserve, particularly in the immunotherapy era [44–46]. Additional markers of hepatic function and portal hypertension may further refine risk stratification in select clinical contexts. The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, although primarily utilized in transplant allocation, may provide complementary prognostic information in patients with advanced liver dysfunction [44]. Surrogate markers of portal hypertension, such as thrombocytopenia and the presence of varices, also influence treatment selection and bleeding risk, particularly in patients considered for anti-angiogenic therapies. While multiple models exist, liver function remains a central determinant of therapeutic decision-making. Importantly, hepatic reserve is dynamic, and longitudinal changes may significantly impact treatment tolerability, risk of toxicity, and eligibility for subsequent therapies.

Underlying hepatic reserve is an important determinant of prognosis, often exerting as much or more influence on overall survival than tumor burden or choice of systemic therapy. Cirrhosis-related complications constrain the intensity, sequence, and tolerability of treatment. The Child-Pugh (CP) score remains the most widely used tool to stage hepatic reserve in cirrhosis. It incorporates five parameters: serum bilirubin, serum albumin, international normalized ratio, presence and severity of ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy [44]. These are combined into a composite score stratified as Child-Pugh A (CPA), B (CPB), or C (CPC). This system is partly subjective, as two of its components, ascites and encephalopathy, depend on clinical judgment.

All pivotal systemic therapy trials for advanced HCC enrolled patients with CPA cirrhosis [10,11,14,15, 23,28]. In everyday practice, however, a substantial proportion of patients present with CPB or CPC disease, where survival and tolerability are markedly worse and high-quality prospective data are limited [47]. Multiple data sets show inferior outcomes in HCC patients with CPB compared to CPA. A meta-analysis of 22 studies reported mOS of 5.5 months with ICIs in HCC patients with CPB cirrhosis and a > 2-fold higher mortality risk (HR 2.33, 95% CI 1.81–2.99) compared to CPA [48]. Subgroup analyses did not demonstrate a significant survival difference between B7 and B8/9 [48]. A large retrospective cohort provided a long-term context with 5-year OS 11.6% in B7, 13.6% in B8, and 8.3% in B9 [49]. Patients with CPB liver cirrhosis have inferior outcomes with reduced median overall survival [50]. The incidence of grade ≥3 adverse events was 15.8% in CPA patients versus 44.4% in CPB patients [51].

The CHALLENGE trial prospectively evaluated atezolizumab plus bevacizumab in patients with unresectable HCC and CP-B7/8 cirrhosis. The study found that the mOS was reduced to 15.4 months in CP-B7/8, and grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 43% compared with 18% in CPA [52]. Almost no benefit was observed in CPC where median OS was 2.5 months [53]. The STRIDE regimen is an important frontline option in CPA but no prospective data exist for CPB or CPC patients. Although real-world studies such as the SIERRA study suggest feasibility in CPB, the efficacy outcomes are pending [54]. SIERRA evaluated the STRIDE regimen as first-line therapy in patients with CPB7-B8 and poor performance status. In the initial analysis, grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events within 6 months occurred in approximately 19% of patients. This overall safety profile was comparable to that seen in HIMALAYA despite worse baseline hepatic function and performance status. Similarly, ipilimumab-nivolumab has shown durable benefit in CPA but prospective CPB data are lacking, and survival outcomes in this group remain undefined.

Notably, nivolumab monotherapy was evaluated in CPB patients [47]. In CheckMate-040 Cohort 5, nivolumab monotherapy was assessed in CP-B7/8 patients, showing an objective response rate of 12% and safety comparable to CPA patients. Prospective clinical trial data in CPB patients treated with nivolumab showed A mOS of 7.6 months was also reported [47].

Among TKIs as well, liver function plays a significant role in efficacy outcomes [12]. In a prospective cohort study of lenvatinib, the median overall survival was substantially poorer in Child-Pugh B patients (4.1 months) compared with results from REFLECT trial in patients with Child-Pugh A, who achieved a median overall survival of 19.7 months [55].

Similarly, the GIDEON registry reported an mOS of 13.6 months for CPA versus 5.2 months for CPB among patients treated with sorafenib [56]. In the post-sorafenib setting, second-line TKIs also demonstrate meaningful activity primarily in CPA populations. For cabozantinib, mOS was 9.7 months in CPA compared with 3.4 months in CPB [13,57]. Regorafenib yielded mOS outcomes of 10.6 to 15.5 months in CPA (RESORCE trial) [11]. The REFINE registry reported mOS of 6.3 months in CPB patients treated with regorafenib [58]. For ramucirumab, mOS in CPA patients was 10.3 months, compared with 6.7 months in those with CPB or CPC [42].

Tislelizumab has been evaluated as both a first- and second-line therapy in unresectable HCC. In the phase II RATIONALE-208 trial of previously treated patients with advanced or metastatic HCC tislelizumab achieved a mOS of 13.2 months [59]. In the first-line setting, the phase III RATIONALE-301 study demonstrated non-inferiority of tislelizumab compared to sorafenib, with a mOS of 15.9 versus 14.1 months, respectively, and a significantly lower rate of grade 3 or higher TRAEs (22% vs. 53% with sorafenib) [60]. However, evidence in patients with impaired liver function remains sparse. The ongoing HESTA trial is specifically designed to evaluate tislelizumab in CPB with ALBI grade 1–2 [61] (Table 2).

The ALBI score uses two objective labs, serum albumin and bilirubin, to quantify hepatic reserves and offers a more precise stratification of liver function [46,65]. It is calculated as a continuous metric and grouped into three prognostic grades: ALBI 1 (≤ 2.60), ALBI 2 (> –2.60 to ≤ –1.39), and ALBI 3 (> –1.39) [65]. ALBI grade exhibits high concordance with traditional CP-score while providing further resolution of liver function. Majority of HCC patients with CP A cirrhosis have ALBI grade 2 liver dysfunction with mOS of 14.7 months compared to 24.5 months with ALBI grade 1 [65]. In a large international validation cohort, ALBI demonstrated clear prognostic discrimination, with survival decreasing stepwise from grade 1 through grade 3 [65].

In a post‑hoc analysis of IMbrave150 stratified by baseline ALBI grade, atezolizumab-bevacizumab significantly improved OS in patients with ALBI 1 (OS HR 0.50, 95% CI: 0.35–0.72) relative to sorafenib [66]. However, no such benefit was observed in ALBI 2 (OS 11.7 vs 12.2 HR: 0.92, 95% CI: 0.66–1.29) [66]. Notably, atezolizumab‑bevacizumab also delayed liver function decline (median time to ALBI 10.2 vs. 8.6 months with sorafenib) [66]. In the updated 5-year analysis of HIMALAYA, the STRIDE regimen showed durable survival overall, with baseline ALBI remaining as a decisive prognostic factor [67]. The 5-year OS rate was 24.3% in ALBI 1 versus 13.7% in ALBI 2/3 [67]. STRIDE regimen demonstrated benefit in 5-year OS regardless of liver function status (ALBI 1 Vs 2/3) and while preserving liver function over time.

ALBI also outperforms Child-Pugh in several retrospective series predicting toxicity and survival with locoregional therapies such as transarterial radioembolization (TARE) and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) [45,68]. For example, survival in patients treated with TARE stratified by ALBI (ALBI 1 ≈ 29 months, ALBI 2 ≈ 13 months, and ALBI 3 ≈ 11 months) and other studies corroborate that ALBI grade outperforms Child-Pugh in prognostic performance [45]. Although there aren’t large prospective trials that exclusively use ALBI grade to stratify patients, there is enough evidence to support its incorporation into trial designs and clinical decision-making frameworks [45].

A novel biomarker that combines ALBI and C-reactive protein (the CALLY score) is being evaluated (NCT06934070) to predict recurrence following curative therapy. The rationale lies in capturing two independent but complementary prognostic axes in HCC. ALBI quantifies hepatic reserve (tolerance and immune competence), while C-reactive protein serves as a surrogate tumor-host inflammation. Integrating these orthogonal axes may refine risk stratification beyond either alone [69].

Unlike the Child-Pugh score, which combines laboratory values with the partly subjective assessment of ascites and encephalopathy, ALBI is an objective continuous measure derived solely from albumin and bilirubin and may detect smaller longitudinal changes in hepatic reserve. The two scores are complementary rather than interchangeable. During active systemic therapy, ALBI and Child-Pugh status should be reassessed before each treatment cycle or approximately every 2–4 weeks, and additionally after bleeding, infection, hospitalization, new ascites or encephalopathy, or a clinically important bilirubin increase.

Worsening Child-Pugh class, progression from ALBI grade 1 to 2/3, development of clinically significant ascites, encephalopathy or rising bilirubin should prompt reassessment of treatment suitability and consideration of dose modification, treatment interruption, or transition to alternative strategies. These recommendations are based primarily on expert consensus and real-world practice rather than prospective trial data.

Beyond hepatic reserve, treatment decisions in advanced HCC should account for patient-related characteristics that directly influence safety, tolerability, and survival outcomes with systemic therapies. This section highlights these key factors and their role in guiding individualized management (Figure 2).

Portal hypertension refers to elevated pressure within the portal venous system, typically defined by a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) ≥5 mm Hg, with clinically significant portal hypertension denoting HVPG ≥10 mm Hg. Portal hypertension increases hemorrhagic risk and may contraindicate anti-VEGF therapy even when varices are not documented [70]. The hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) remains the gold standard but is not routinely available in clinical practice [71]. Instead, noninvasive surrogates such as platelet count and liver stiffness measurement (LSM) are used [71]. The Baveno VII consensus (platelets ≥150 × 109/L and liver stiffness <15 kPa rule out; liver stiffness ≥25 kPa to rule in clinically significant portal hypertension, provides a practical triage to determine patients who require baseline EGD prior to anti-VEGF therapy [72,73]. Although the LSM plus platelet criteria were originally developed in patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease, subsequent retrospective studies have evaluated these surrogates in HCC populations. However, they have not been prospectively validated as standalone predictors of bevacizumab associated bleeding in patients with HCC.

This criteria can provide a framework for decision making on choosing a therapeutic regimen in frontline setting [72,73]. Portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT) is a distinct high-risk context that often coexists with clinically significant portal hypertension and fragile varices [74]. Patients with PVTT may be at an increased risk of variceal bleeding, particularly with anti-VEGF therapies. In real-world practice, screening for varices is essential before initiating anti-VEGF therapy.

Gastroesophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins that develop as a consequence of portal hypertension, caused by elevated pressure and resistance within the portal venous system. These fragile vessels are prone to rupture and life-threatening hemorrhage, particularly in the setting of clinically significant portal hypertension or PVTT. IMbrave150 allowed patients with PVTT and esophagogastric varices, provided they underwent endoscopic evaluation within 6 months and any varices at risk of bleeding were treated according to institutional standards before starting bevacizumab. Patients with untreated or incompletely treated, high-risk esophageal or gastric varices were excluded. High-risk varices are typically defined by the Baveno VII and AASLD criteria as large varices (>5 mm in diameter), varices with red wale signs or those in patients with advanced liver disease (Child-Pugh B/C) who have not received prophylactic therapy [71]. Despite these precautions, upper gastrointestinal bleeding occurred more often with atezolizumab-bevacizumab compared to sorafenib (7% vs 4.5%) [75]. Prospective and real-world studies suggest even higher risk with one-year cumulative incidence approaching ∼20% with IMBRAVE 150 regimen compared to 5% with sorafenib [70]. A prior history of variceal bleeding was the strongest predictor of variceal bleed (HR 10.58), while other risk factors included high body mass index, ALBI grade 3, and PVTT [70].

From a practical standpoint, patients being considered for bevacizumab should undergo risk stratification for portal hypertension and variceal bleeding prior to treatment initiation. Baveno VII provides a useful noninvasive triage framework for patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease [71]. Clinically significant portal hypertension is unlikely when liver stiffness measurement by transient elastography is ≤15 kPa and platelet count is ≥150 × 109/L [71]. Conversely, patients with liver stiffness ≥20 kPa or platelet count ≤150 × 109/L should undergo screening endoscopy to evaluate for varices requiring treatment. However, these criteria were developed primarily for compensated chronic liver disease rather than specifically for patients with HCC. Therefore, in patients with HCC being considered for anti-VEGF therapy, Baveno VII criteria should be viewed as an initial triage tool rather than a substitute for individualized bleeding-risk assessment. Endoscopic evaluation should still be strongly considered in patients with additional risk factors, including prior variceal hemorrhage, PVTT, thrombocytopenia, deteriorating liver function, radiographic features of portal hypertension, or other clinical concern for high-risk varices [76]. High-risk varices should be treated according to current guideline recommendations before initiation of anti-VEGF therapy. A prior history of variceal bleeding does not necessarily preclude bevacizumab use, however, these patients represent a particularly high-risk population and require close monitoring.

In practical terms, bevacizumab may be considered when a prior variceal bleeding episode has been successfully controlled, high-risk varices have been eradicated or adequately treated with endoscopic variceal ligation and/or nonselective beta-blockers, recent upper endoscopy confirms no untreated high-risk varices, the patient is clinically stable without active or very recent bleeding, portal hypertension is reasonably controlled, liver function remains adequate, and the decision is made after multidisciplinary review involving oncology, hepatology, and/or gastroenterology [70]. Conversely, bevacizumab should generally be avoided or deferred in the setting of active variceal bleeding, untreated or incompletely treated high-risk varices, recent endoscopic variceal ligation before mucosal healing, recurrent bleeding despite appropriate prophylaxis, or severe portal hypertension with very high bleeding risk. Many experts recommend waiting at least 14 days after variceal ligation before initiating atezolizumab-bevacizumab because post-ligation bleeding risk is highest early after the procedure [75]. When bleeding risk remains prohibitive despite optimization, VEGF-free immunotherapy such as STRIDE, durvalumab monotherapy, or nivolumab/ipilimumab, or TKI monotherapy, may be preferred depending on liver function, tumor burden, and patient-specific comorbidities.

Compared with bevacizumab, TKIs appear to carry a lower incidence of major bleeding, though the risk is not negligible. In the SHARP trial, GI bleeding occurred in 2% of sorafenib-treated patients versus 4% with placebo [75]. In REFLECT, grade 3–5 GI bleeding occurred in 5% with lenvatinib, and variceal bleeding in large real-world cohorts occurred in 3% at 12 months when endoscopic prophylaxis was routine [77]. High-risk varices warrant primary prophylaxis with a nonselective β-blocker or endoscopic variceal ligation per Baveno VII/AASLD guidance [71]. Carvedilol is favored because it combines β1/β2 and α1 antagonism, yielding greater HVPG reductions and lower first-bleed risk versus propranolol, with a typical target dose of 12.5 mg/day as tolerated (monitor BP/renal function) [78]. If carvedilol is contraindicated or not tolerated, ligation can be performed [79]. If high-risk features persist despite optimization, VEGF-free immunotherapy (e.g., Nivolumab/Ipilimumab, STRIDE or durvalumab) or TKI monotherapy is preferred [34].

Portal venous thrombosis (PVT) is thrombus within the portal vein or its branches and constitutes another key prognostic factor in the management of patients with HCC [80]. Distinction between portal vein tumor thrombus (PVTT) caused by intravascular extension of viable HCC vs bland thrombus (non-tumoral clot) is essential. PVTT denotes macrovascular invasion and carries adverse biology and bleeding risk, independent of tumor burden.

The Liver Cancer Study Group of Japan (LCSGJ) classification stratifies PVTT into five categories based on the extent of vascular invasion [80]. Vp0 indicates no tumor thrombus. Vp1 refers to thrombus confined to segmental or distal branches beyond the second-order portal vein. Vp2 involves the second-order branches, while Vp3 extends into a first-order branch (either the right or left portal vein). Vp4 denotes thrombus within the main portal trunk and/or extension into the contralateral branch to the primarily involved lobe (or both). In a treatment-naïve Western cohort with PVTT, mOS across modalities declined from Vp1 to Vp4 [81].

In IMbrave150, the proportions of patients with PVTT sub categories were: Vp1 8%, Vp2 14%, Vp3 16%, and Vp4 14% in the atezolizumab‐bevacizumab arm [82]. Patients with VP4 PVTT demonstrated outcomes favoring the combination regimen, with a mOS of 7.6 months (95% CI 6.0–13.9) vs 5.5 months (95% CI 3.4–6.7) for sorafenib (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.34–1.11) [82]. This elucidates the poor prognostic impact of VP4 PVTT with a significant decline in mOS outcomes compared to patients without Vp4 involvement with mOS of 21.1 months for atezolizumab-bevacizumab versus 15.4 months for sorafenib [82].

The HIMALAYA and CheckMate-9DW trial excluded patients with Vp4 PVTT [28]. However, patients with lesser degrees of invasion (Vp1-Vp3) were still eligible. Published data did not report survival outcomes stratified by Vp subclass in either of these trials. For Vp1-Vp3 PVTT, no randomized evidence demonstrates that PVTT subclass alone should determine selection of an anti-VEGF containing regimen versus VEGF-free dual immunotherapy. Patients with Vp1-Vp3 disease were eligible for IMbrave150, HIMALAYA, and CheckMate 9DW. Regimen selection should therefore integrate the extent of vascular invasion with variceal status, platelet count, hepatic reserve, anticoagulation requirements, and overall bleeding risk. Vp4 disease should be considered separately because IMbrave150 included patients with main portal vein thrombosis and reported outcomes in this subgroup, whereas HIMALAYA and CheckMate 9DW excluded patients with main portal vein thrombosis.

Anti-VEGF therapy worsens hypertension and impairs wound healing. In patients treated with atezolizumab-bevacizumab, hypertension affected over 30% of the patients [34,83]. Across solid tumors, ICIs were associated with higher cardiovascular toxicity, any cardiotoxicity 3.0% vs 2.3% (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.17–1.48), including increased risks of myocarditis (RR 1.79) and arrhythmia (RR 1.22) [84]. The risk was further increased when ICIs were combined with anti-angiogenics, showing roughly a 25% higher odds of grade 3–4 hypertension compared with monotherapy [83]. Across frontline HCC trials, grade ≥3 hypertension occurred in 15.2% with atezolizumab-bevacizumab, and 1.8% with STRIDE [15]. In patients with cardiovascular comorbidity or labile blood pressure, anti-VEGF regimens should be considered with caution, and VEGF-free immunotherapy or TKIs may be reasonable options [85]. There are emerging instruments like the CARDIOSOR scale that provide for personalized cardiovascular risk stratification [86]. The CARDIOSOR score is a pragmatic bedside tool originally developed for sorafenib-treated HCC patients, incorporating age, classic cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia) and prior arterial disease (ischemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral artery disease) to stratify patients into low- and high-risk categories for cardiovascular events.

Patients classified as high cardiovascular risk but without an ICI specific contraindication should undergo baseline cardiovascular or cardio-oncology evaluation, optimization of hypertension, heart failure and ischemic disease, and review of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy. High baseline cardiovascular risk alone is not a contraindication to checkpoint blockade. However, active myocarditis, unstable ischemia, decompensated heart failure, or another uncontrolled cardiovascular condition warrants treatment deferral and specialist assessment. With this risk framework established, we next address common clinical situations and their implications on regimen choice. The following recommendations are derived from available cardio-oncology guidance and anti-VEGF safety data. Given the limited prospective HCC-specific evidence in this area, these proposed time intervals should be considered pragmatic considerations rather than definitive evidence-based thresholds.

In high-bleeding-risk patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with contemporary drug eluting stent (DES), dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) can be shortened to 1–3 months [87]. After 1–3 months of DAPT, transitioning to P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy has been shown to reduce bleeding risk without increasing ischemic events [87]. VEGF inhibitors increase the risk of bleeding and thrombotic events [88]. IMbrave150 excluded patients with recent myocardial infarction or stroke within 6 months, and any thromboembolism within 3 months due to bleeding and vascular safety concerns [27,89]. In contrast, HIMALAYA did not specify time based exclusion criteria for prior myocardial infarction, stroke or venous thromboembolism. Instead, it broadly excluded patients with clinically significant or unstable cardiac disease, leaving vascular risk mostly to investigator judgment [27,89,90]. CheckMate 9DW excluded patients with a myocardial infarction within 6 months [27,89,90]. Lenvatinib labeling explicitly states it has not been studied after arterial thromboembolism within 6 months [91]. European Society of Cardiology (ESC) recommends performing baseline CV risk assessment and multi-disciplinary decision making around pro-thrombotic and high bleeding risk anticancer therapies [91].

sections.title: 0–90 days after percutaneous coronary intervention (on DAPT)

paragraphs.en: This period carries the highest combined bleeding and ischemic risk. Patients are typically maintained on DAPT, and the addition of anti-VEGF is unfavorable due to additive bleeding risk [87]. Current data support shortening DAPT duration to 1 month when feasible in patients with high risk for bleeding [87]. It is reasonable to consider VEGF-free alternatives during 0–90 days post PCI.

Once DAPT has been de-escalated to single antiplatelet therapy and there have been no recurrent ischemic events, consideration of immunotherapy combinations can be individualized [87,91]. Anti-VEGF use may still pose risk if hypertension or proteinuria persist. European Society of Cardiology recommends approximately 6 months after a major arterial event as a safety boundary before reintroducing anti-VEGF therapy [91].
Beyond 6 months, anti-VEGF therapy can generally be re-introduced comfortably provided the patient has stable cardiovascular status [91].

Wound-healing impairment is a known side-effect of anti-VEGF therapy. For bevacizumab, it is recommended to hold for 4–6 weeks prior to elective surgery and to resume 28 days after major surgery and when wounds have fully healed. Meta-analyses link perioperative bevacizumab exposure with increased postoperative wound complications, supporting these intervals [92]. If systemic therapy is absolutely required, VEGF-free ICI regimens (such as durvalumab-tremelimumab or nivolumab-ipilimumab) are preferred. Once grafts are stable, wounds are healed, and antiplatelet therapy has been de-escalated, anti-VEGF therapy may be reintroduced with strict monitoring and multidisciplinary oversight [91].

Bevacizumab’s bleeding risk is both dose- and tumor-type dependent. Concomitant antiplatelets may further augment the risk. The safest strategy while on DAPT is to avoid anti-VEGF and use ICI only or ICI combination therapy until DAPT is shortened/stopped (often at 1–3 months in high bleeding risk patients with modern DES).

IMbrave150, HIMALAYA and CheckMate-9DW clinical trials commonly excluded patients with significant, unstable cardiovascular disease [27,89]. Society of Cardiology has mandated baseline risk stratification and surveillance (echo) before administering such therapy [91].

In patients with NYHA class III-IV HF or decompensated HF, consider avoiding anti-VEGF therapies (including bevacizumab, ramucirumab and TKIs) given their adverse effects of hypertension and elevated risk of vascular ischemia [91]. If systemic therapy cannot be deferred, VEGF-free ICI regimens (such as durvalumab-tremelimumab or nivolumab-ipilimumab) can be considered after shared decision making with the patient.

Many patients with advanced HCC require anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, or portal vein thrombosis. Data regarding the safety of concurrent direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) and anti-VEGF therapy remain limited, particularly in patients with portal hypertension and varices. Data are even more limited regarding the concomitant use of DOACs with antiplatelet agents in patients with HCC receiving bevacizumab [93,94]. Anticoagulation should not be considered an absolute contraindication to anti-VEGF-containing therapy. Small retrospective studies suggest that DOAC therapy alone may not substantially increase severe bleeding risk in carefully selected patients treated with atezolizumab-bevacizumab; however, evidence regarding combined anticoagulant-antiplatelet therapy remains sparse. Therefore, bleeding risk should be assessed on an individual basis with careful consideration of variceal status, prior bleeding history, liver function, thrombocytopenia, and the indication for anticoagulation. Given the bleeding risk associated with VEGF inhibition and the additive bleeding concerns of combined antithrombotic therapy, patients receiving a DOAC together with antiplatelet agents should be considered at heightened risk for gastrointestinal and variceal bleeding. Multidisciplinary collaboration involving oncology, hepatology, gastroenterology, and cardiology may be helpful in complex cases.

Preexisting autoimmune diseases (AID) have previously been shown to increase the risk of flares and immune-related adverse events (irAEs) [95]. Patients with active AID were largely excluded from trials, and emerging data indicates increased risks of autoimmune flares. Retrospective series report grade 3–4 IBD flares exceeding 20% and an overall 2–3-fold increase in significant irAEs with active AID [95,96]. It is for this reason that patients with uncontrolled AID and those on medications are not appropriate candidates for ICIs [97]. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors may be considered in selected patients with active autoimmune disease because they do not carry the same risk of immune-mediated disease flare.

However, TKIs should not be considered risk free alternatives. There is no established evidence of autoimmune “cross-reactivity” comparable to that associated with ICIs, but TKI related hepatic, cardiovascular, renal, dermatologic, and gastrointestinal toxicities may overlap with or exacerbate organ involvement from an active autoimmune disease [98]. Decisions should be made through shared decision making with the patient, balancing benefits and risks and in close collaboration and follow up with the relevant subspecialist, typically rheumatology when preexisting AID or rheumatic irAEs are present [32].

Management of HCC recurrence after liver transplantation is challenging due to risk of allograft rejection with ICIs. Major guidelines (ESMO, AASLD, NCCN) advise caution with ICI use in this setting given acute rejection rates from 28 to 32%, with some cases progressing to catastrophic graft loss. Among 8 post live transplant patients treated with atezolizumab for recurrent HCC, 25% developed rejection and 75% died during follow-up (mOS 6.2 months) [99]. An atezolizumab specific median time to rejection cannot be reliably estimated from this series because only two of eight patients developed rejection and a median onset interval was not reported. In broader analyses of solid organ transplant recipients treated with ICIs, rejection has generally occurred early, with pooled median onset estimates of approximately 21–24 days after ICI initiation [100]. These findings reinforce that no duration of post-transplant ICI exposure can currently be considered established as safe.

A recent meta-analysis reported a 25% graft rejection rate and a 75% mortality rate after ICI in post-liver-transplant patients with recurrent malignancy [99]. In pooled analyses of 28 solid organ transplant recipients (mostly liver), rejection occurred in ∼32% of cases while response rates remained modest at ∼25%, underscoring the narrow therapeutic margin [101]. ESMO and AASLD highlight limited data and recommend TKIs as preferred first-line agents[102,103]. Prospective clinical trials are underway in this subpopulation: NCT03966209 which is evaluating the role of PD-1 inhibitors in liver-transplant recipients with recurrent/metastatic malignancies. NCT04564313 is another trial that is evaluating the role of camrelizumab in recurrent HCC after liver transplant in China.

Clinical decision-making in this context must therefore be individualized and centered around patient preferences after detailed discussion of risks and benefits [104]. A preliminary framework for making decisions includes the following: (i) careful patient selection (focus on performance status and disease burden), (ii) baseline evaluation of graft immunogenicity, including PD-L1 expression where feasible (iii) maintaining or modifying immunosuppression and (iv) close monitoring with early rejection detection.

Historically, bridging and downstaging pre-LT have relied on almost entirely on locoregional (TACE, ablation, Y-90) therapies [105]. In routine practice, US registry data show that locoregional therapies (LRT) remains the dominant approach [106]. Among >24,000 LT candidates with HCC (2003–2018), 92.4% received at least one LRT while waiting [106]. Chemoembolization was the first LRT in 66%, thermal ablation in 20%, and radioembolization rose to 19% by 2018. By contrast, systemic therapy as a bridge remains a minority practice [106].

Systemic therapies (especially ICIs) were previously considered contraindicated because of reports of acute, sometimes fatal rejection and the theoretical risk of immune activation across the graft. Current consensus therefore advises restricting pre-LT ICI strategies to specialized centers with careful selection and a defined washout period [107]. The literature of pre-LT ICIs to date comprises on the order of a few hundred patients globally reflecting select-center adoption rather than standard of care [108].

The VITALITY study was a prospective cohort evaluating the use of ICIs as downstaging or bridging therapy for patients with HCC initially beyond Milan criteria but otherwise potential candidates for LT [108]. In this study, 75.6% were downstaged with ICIs from beyond Milan within a median 5.6 months and 36.7% underwent LT [108]. Acute rejection mostly clustered when washout was less than 3 months [108].

Current evidence suggests aiming for a washout of at least 3 months, though multicenter analyses suggest that >50 days may be acceptable when longer delays are not feasible [109]. The approximately 3-month washout discussed here applies specifically to ICIs and is intended to reduce the risk of post-transplant allograft rejection. It should not be extrapolated to bevacizumab or oral TKIs, which require separate pharmacokinetic and perioperative considerations. For bevacizumab, the principal concerns are bleeding and impaired wound healing. Due to this, labeling requires a minimum interval of 28 days before major surgery, while many transplant centers use a longer interval, commonly 6–8 weeks, because of its prolonged half-life. Oral TKIs generally require shorter, agent specific perioperative holds. The final interval should therefore be drug-specific and determined jointly by the oncology and transplant teams.

Regimen selection should align with the patient’s ability and support for travel and infusion frequency. Atezolizumab-bevacizumab is administered every 3 weeks, STRIDE uses a single tremelimumab dose followed by durvalumab, every 4 weeks. Ipilimumab-nivolumab involves an induction phase every 3 weeks followed by maintenance nivolumab, and TKIs are commonly administered orally on a daily schedule.

Patients with transportation barriers, limited access to tertiary or academic centers, or financial and caregiving constraints may face practical challenges in receiving infusion-based care. These challenges may push patients and providers to make difficult decisions about type and/or sequencing of available systemic therapy options. In patients facing significant logistical or financial barriers to frequent infusions, the choice between VEGF-ICI combinations, ICI-only regimens, and oral TKIs should be individualized. Systemic therapy selection must account not only for tumor biology and liver function but also for performance status, comorbidities, patient preferences, and access to care, including the potential for financial toxicity. Oral TKIs may be considered among the available options when they align with the patient’s goals and practical ability to adhere to treatment, recognizing that they also carry cost and toxicity burdens. Ultimately, treatment selection should be guided by shared decision-making that integrates tumor-related prognostic factors with the patient’s functional status and real-world ability to receive and sustain systemic therapy.

In resource-limited settings, affordability and reliable access should be treated as clinical feasibility variables rather than secondary considerations. The relevant comparison is the total cost of care, including drug acquisition, infusion infrastructure, endoscopic assessment, travel, laboratory monitoring, management of toxicity, and hospitalization, rather than drug price alone [110]. Where available and clinically appropriate, oral TKIs particularly lower cost generic formulations may reduce infusion-related logistical burden [110]. Cost driven selection should be transparent, incorporated into shared decision-making, and should not imply that a less costly regimen is biologically equivalent to an otherwise preferred ICI combination.

The FDA had approved subcutaneous (SC) atezolizumab for all adult indications of the IV formulation, including HCC. Subcutaneous nivolumab was also recently approved across most solid-tumor nivolumab indications including HCC. For patients initiated on CheckMate-9DW (IV nivolumab + IV ipilimumab), the combination phase should remain IV, but SC nivolumab may be used during nivolumab maintenance monotherapy per labeling. Operationally, SC delivery can reduce chair time (3–5 minutes for SC) versus 30 minutes IV infusions and may improve patient satisfaction [111].

Although not currently used in routine clinical decision-making, anti-drug antibodies (ADAs) have emerged as a potential biomarker that may influence future treatment selection and therapeutic monitoring. ADAs are patient derived antibodies. They arise when a patient’s immune system mounts B-cell/T-cell dependent responses against a therapeutic protein. “Binding” ADAs form immune complexes that accelerate target-drug clearance and lower exposure, whereas “neutralizing” antibodies directly block target engagement [112]. In oncology specifically, ADAs may reduce drug exposure resulting in reduced drug efficacy, but clinical impact is inconsistent across agents and trials. Reported ADA rates vary widely because assay sensitivity, sampling schedules, drug interference, and patient/disease factors all influence detection and titers.

In IMbrave 150, 28% of patients developed treatment emergent atezolizumab ADAs by week 6, and ADA-positive patients appeared to derive less OS benefit than ADA-negative patients in exploratory analyses (HR vs sorafenib 0.93 vs 0.39). In contrast, bevacizumab ADAs are rare (∼0.6% in adjuvant solid tumor studies) with unclear significance. In HIMALAYA, ADAs developed in 2.9% of patients receiving durvalumab and 11% receiving tremelimumab, with no clear impact on efficacy reported. For nivolumab, pooled model-informed analyses across many trials suggest 16% ADA with monotherapy and 32% when combined with ipilimumab (neutralizing rare) [113]. For ipilimumab, ADA rates around 6–13% have been described (neutralizing rare). CheckMate 9DW has not yet reported ADA data. On the other hand, small molecule TKIs (lenvatinib and sorafenib) are not subject to ADA related immunogenicity risk [114]. At present, routine ADA testing is not recommended in clinical practice, and prospective studies are needed before ADA-guided treatment strategies can be incorporated into routine care.

Despite major advances in systemic therapies for advanced HCC, validated predictive biomarkers are still lacking [115]. For ICIs, markers such as PD-L1 expression, intratumoral CD8 density and FOXP3 regulatory T-cell infiltration have shown inconsistent predictive value for treatment response across studies [115]. Unfortunately, TMB as a predictive biomarker hasn’t translated to improved outcomes in HCC with multiple analyses show no dependable link between TMB‑high status and ICI benefit in HCC [115]. This is largely due to the immune heterogeneity of HCC and its tumor microenvironment [116]. Instead, activation of the WNT/β-catenin (CTNNB1) pathway could be a potential negative predictor, driving immune exclusion and primary resistance to ICIs [116]. However, no validated companion diagnostic or routinely recommended clinical assay currently exists for using WNT/β-catenin status to select or exclude patients from ICI therapy in HCC. Testing therefore remains investigational or part of broader molecular profiling and should not be used as a stand-alone reason to withhold immunotherapy [116].

In the phase Ib/II MORPHEUS-Liver randomized signal-seeking study, adding the anti-TIGIT (T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains) antibody tiragolumab to atezolizumab-bevacizumab increased response rates versus atezolizumab-bevacizumab alone, suggesting on-target activity in advanced HCC [117]. These findings prompted the phase III IMbrave152/SKYSCRAPER-14 trial, that failed to meet its primary endpoints (no PFS or OS benefit) [118]. Collectively, TIGIT expression or pathway readouts are not ready for primetime treatment selection in HCC.

For TKIs, exploratory studies suggest that VEGFA amplification and FGF3/FGF4 gains may be associated with increased sensitivity, whereas activation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway confers resistance [119]. For lenvatinib, higher baseline levels of serum VEGF and angiopoietin-2 (ANG2) are associated with poorer outcomes, while elevated FGF21 has been proposed as a candidate predictive marker of relative benefit compared to sorafenib [120].

Emerging molecular biomarkers may further refine prognostication. For example, higher Vav1 expression has been associated with advanced disease and inferior overall survival, while PRDX6 has been linked to tumor proliferation and survival through pathways such as PI3K/Akt/mTOR [121,122]. Although these markers remain investigational, they highlight the potential role of molecular profiling in enhancing personalized treatment strategies. Recent bioinformatics-driven analyses have further identified several candidate hub genes and molecular networks associated with HCC progression, immune regulation, and therapeutic resistance, highlighting the growing potential of molecular profiling to inform personalized treatment strategies [123,124]. Additionally, emerging preclinical evidence suggests that microRNA-mediated regulation of ferroptosis-related pathways may contribute to tumor progression. While these findings remain exploratory, they underscore the expanding landscape of molecular biomarkers that may refine prognostication in future studies.

Liquid biopsy approaches rely on the detection of circulating tumor-derived components such as circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells, and extracellular vesicles, offering a noninvasive method to assess tumor biology and dynamics [125]. These techniques have the potential to improve early detection, prognostication, and treatment monitoring. However, their routine clinical implementation is limited by factors such as variable sensitivity, particularly in early-stage disease and the need for further validation in large prospective studies.

The management of HCC is influenced not only by patient-related factors but also by significant regional variations in healthcare infrastructure and guideline adoption. While major international guidelines such as those from National Comprehensive Cancer Network, European Society for Medical Oncology, and American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases broadly align on the use of ICI-based combinations in the frontline setting, their real-world implementation varies considerably across geographic regions [36,102,103].

In high-income countries, access to combination ICI regimens is generally feasible, allowing for guideline-concordant care. In contrast, in low- and middle-income countries, limited access to immunotherapy, cost constraints, and healthcare infrastructure challenges often necessitate reliance on TKIs such as sorafenib or lenvatinib, even in the frontline setting.

Evidence supporting sequential TKI therapy is derived primarily from pre-ICI studies rather than studies designed specifically for low- and middle-income countries. In an exploratory analysis of RESORCE, selected patients who tolerated sorafenib and subsequently received regorafenib had a median survival of 26.0 months from initiation of sorafenib, compared with 19.2 months among those subsequently receiving placebo [126]. However, this population retained CPA liver function, tolerated prior sorafenib, and remained sufficiently fit for second-line therapy. The finding therefore supports the feasibility of sequential TKI treatment in selected patients but does not establish a universal low-cost strategy, particularly because the affordability and availability of regorafenib vary substantially by region.

Furthermore, access to multidisciplinary care, transplant programs, and locoregional therapies varies significantly, impacting eligibility for curative or bridging strategies. Consequently, while the proposed clinical framework provides a structured approach to personalized treatment selection, its application must be contextualized within regional resource availability.

While many of these patient subgroups are discussed in detail in the above sections, it is important to emphasize several overarching principles that guide treatment selection in special populations. Patients with autoimmune disease, cardiovascular comorbidities, prior liver transplantation, or poor performance status are often underrepresented in clinical trials, and treatment decisions must therefore rely on real-world evidence and individualized risk assessment. In patients with poor performance status, less intensive approaches or supportive care may be appropriate. These considerations highlight the importance of multidisciplinary evaluation and shared decision-making in optimizing outcomes.

In parallel, emerging applications of artificial intelligence and big data are beginning to influence clinical decision-making in HCC. Radiomics-based approaches have shown potential in predicting treatment response and survival outcomes through quantitative imaging analysis [127]. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and other liquid biopsy techniques may further refine disease monitoring and early detection of resistance [125]. Additionally, machine learning models integrating imaging, genomic, and clinical parameters, including liver function, are being developed to enhance prognostication and guide individualized treatment selection. However, these approaches remain investigational and require prospective validation prior to routine clinical implementation.

Liver transplantation (LT), remains the most effective curative therapy for HCC, addressing both tumor and underlying cirrhosis. The primary goal of downstaging therapy is to reduce tumor burden in initially ineligible patients to within transplant criteria. In contrast, bridging therapy is intended to prevent progression in patients who are already eligible for transplantation but are facing a prolonged waiting period [128].

However, because donor organs are scarce, patient selection relies on validated morphologic criteria to maximize results. Classically, the Milan criteria (one lesion ≤5 cm or three lesions ≤3 cm without macrovascular invasion) has been used and associated with an 83% 4-year recurrence free survival rate [129]. To address the limitations of Milan, several expanded frameworks have been proposed, including the up-to-seven rule, UCSF criteria, and total tumor volume (TTV) based models [130–132].

Candidates for downstaging are those beyond Milan but within accepted UNOS/OPTN downstaging limits, with no macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic disease, and AFP ≤1,000 ng/mL (or decline to <500 ng/mL after treatment). After successful downstaging into Milan, programs confirm radiographic stability ≥4 weeks after the last treatment and generally observe stability for 6 months before exception points are awarded. Bridging is advised when the anticipated wait exceeds 6 months to limit drop-out. MELD-Na informs transplant priority and global hepatic risk, while Child-Pugh (with ALBI refinement) captures functional reserve. Decisions are finalized via multidisciplinary review incorporating ECOG performance status and comorbidities [133].

For bridging to surgical resection, selection includes on preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A), absence of clinically significant portal hypertension (classically HVPG ≤10 mmHg or surrogate markers such as platelets ≥100 × 109/L, no varices), adequate future liver remnant, and ECOG 0–1 [133]. Here, Child-Pugh A and low MELD-Na favor resection, and rising MELD-Na, CP-B/C, or CSPH shifts candidacy toward LT or non-surgical strategies [36,133].

Across both LT and resection pathways, tumor biology (AFP level/trend, radiologic response to therapy, mRECIST/EASL), liver reserve (Child-Pugh, MELD-Na, ALBI), performance status, and comorbidity (cardiovascular, portal hypertension/varices) drive candidacy [36,133]. Current guideline frameworks (AASLD, EASL/BCLC, OPTN) converge on: (i) downstaging when tumor burden is modestly beyond Milan but biologically favorable; (ii) bridging when expected wait is prolonged; and (iii) systematic use of MELD-Na and Child-Pugh/ALBI plus a multidisciplinary review to decide between LT, resection, or systemic therapy when LRT is unsuitable [36,133].

Locoregional therapy (LRT) is the cornerstone for both downstaging and bridging [107,133]. Emerging systemic therapies, particularly ICI-based regimens, are under investigation for their role in downstaging. In the prospective VITALITY study, patients with HCC beyond Milan criteria treated with atezolizumab-bevacizumab achieved successful downstaging in a substantial proportion of cases, allowing a subset to proceed to transplantation with encouraging post-transplant outcomes. However, the use of ICIs before transplantation remains controversial because of the risk of allograft rejection. Available data suggest that rejection risk is highest when transplantation occurs shortly after ICI exposure, and several studies have suggested a washout period of at least 2–3 months before transplantation whenever feasible. Consequently, while ICI-based downstaging represents a promising strategy, patient selection, timing of transplantation, and multidisciplinary coordination remain critical.

However, evidence supporting ICIs as approaches for downstaging or bridging remains preliminary. Such choices should be individualized based on bleeding risk, hepatic reserve, and anticipated tolerance.

This table provides a clinically oriented, patient-centered approach to treatment selection based on key variables including liver function, bleeding risk, autoimmune disease, transplant status, cardiovascular comorbidity, thrombocytopenia, and logistical considerations (Table 3). Recommended therapeutic options are aligned with available evidence and major clinical trials, with emphasis on real-world applicability and multidisciplinary decision-making.

*This is a suggested framework of management of patients with HCC and could vary from patient to patient based on the comorbidities and complexity. Multidisciplinary evaluation with expertise in HCC management is highly recommended. Evaluate for clinical trial eligibility wherever feasible.

Special populations, including pediatric HCC and patients with rare underlying liver diseases, were not specifically addressed in this review. These groups have distinct biological and clinical characteristics and remain underrepresented in the current literature, representing important areas for future investigation.

Additionally, this review is primarily based on data from pivotal clinical trials and guideline recommendations, which may not fully reflect the heterogeneity of real-world patient populations. Although real-world evidence is increasing, it remains limited and heterogeneous, particularly with respect to long-term outcomes and optimal treatment sequencing, underscoring a critical need for further prospective and real-world studies.

No single regimen is optimal for every patient. Personalized treatment selection requires integration of tumor biology, hepatic reserve, bleeding risk, cardiovascular health, transplant considerations, and patient-specific priorities within a multidisciplinary framework.

Over the next 5–10 years, the management of hepatocellular carcinoma is expected to shift further toward precision oncology, with increasing integration of molecular, clinical, and imaging-based biomarkers into treatment decision-making. Advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning are likely to enable more accurate prediction of treatment response and survival by incorporating multidimensional data, including radiomics, genomics, and dynamic liver function parameters. The development of validated predictive biomarkers for immunotherapy response remains a critical unmet need and may facilitate more rational patient selection and sequencing strategies. In parallel, novel therapeutic combinations, including next-generation immune checkpoint inhibitors, bispecific antibodies, and cellular therapies, are expected to expand the treatment landscape. Improved understanding of mechanisms of resistance may also guide more effective post-progression strategies. Additionally, increasing availability of real-world data and pragmatic clinical trials will help bridge the gap between trial populations and routine practice.
